lead: At equilibrium two phases of the same mixture share the same temperature, the same pressure, and the same chemical potential for every component. Chemical potential μ_i is the partial molar Gibbs energy in J/mol. It measures how G changes when a tiny amount of component i is added. Fugacity f_i in Pa is the working variable because μ has no absolute zero. A phase is stable only if its Gibbs energy is a minimum, not merely flat. Distillation, extraction, crystallisation and refinery separations all use these tests.
prereq: You need: Unit 4 (Gibbs energy and fundamental relations) and Unit 5 (chemical potential, fugacity and activity).

blocks.text: Start from the fundamental relation for a closed system of C components: dG = −S dT + V dP + Σ μ_i dn_i. Here G is Gibbs energy in J, S entropy in J/K, T absolute temperature in K, V volume in m³, P pressure in Pa, n_i moles of component i, and μ_i chemical potential in J/mol. μ_i is also the partial molar Gibbs energy: the change in G when one mole of i is added at fixed T, P and other moles. At fixed T and P with no reaction, dG = Σ μ_i dn_i. Transfer dn_i moles of i from phase β to phase α changes G by (μ_i^α − μ_i^β) dn_i. If this is negative, transfer lowers G. Equilibrium needs it zero for every component, so μ_i^α = μ_i^β for every i and every pair of phases. Thermal equilibrium needs T^α = T^β. Mechanical equilibrium needs P^α = P^β. A curved interface can hold a small pressure jump because surface tension supports it.

blocks.where: μ_i is chemical potential in J/mol; μ_i° is the standard chemical potential in J/mol; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is temperature in K; f_i is fugacity in Pa; f_i° is the standard fugacity in Pa. For the same component, the standard term cancels between phases, so μ_i^α = μ_i^β becomes f_i^α = f_i^β.

blocks.text: The fugacity form is the working criterion. It removes the arbitrary reference value inside μ. See 6.2 for counting the variables you may set, and 6.4 for using the equality in vapour-liquid equilibrium.

sections.h3: Stability: a minimum, not a saddle

blocks.text: At fixed T and P, a stable phase has the lowest G. For a binary mixture write g^M/RT = x₁ ln x₁ + x₂ ln x₂ + A x₁x₂. Here g^M is molar Gibbs energy of mixing in J/mol, R is the gas constant, T is in K, x₁ and x₂ are mole fractions, and A is a dimensionless interaction parameter. The first derivative with respect to x₁ is ln(x₁/x₂) + A(1 − 2x₁). Setting it to zero gives a stationary composition. The second derivative is 1/x₁ + 1/x₂ − 2A. Stability requires (∂²G/∂x₁²)_{T,P} > 0, equivalently this expression > 0. The spinodal is the locus where the second derivative is zero. The binodal is the common-tangent line between two coexisting phases; it gives the actual phase compositions. Between binodal and spinodal the mixture is metastable. Inside the spinodal it is unstable: any small composition wave lowers G, so the mixture splits without a nucleation barrier. Some syllabi call the first equality the criterion of equilibrium and this curvature test the criterion of stability.

sections.h3: Using the criteria without mixing up variables

blocks.text: Use the criteria in order. First confirm T and P are equal; for a flat interface this is enough for thermal and mechanical equilibrium. Then write f_i^α = f_i^β for each component; this is one equation per component. Finally check curvature. The equimolar point with A = 2.5 has negative curvature, so it cannot be a single phase even though its first derivative is zero. A = 1.5 gives positive curvature at x₁ = 0.5 and is locally stable. The same algebra appears in liquid-liquid extraction and polymer blends; see 6.7. For pure components the fugacity equality reduces to the vapour-pressure curve; see 6.3.

figure.caption: Gibbs energy of mixing against x₁. The A = 2.5 curve rises in the middle: at x₁ = 0.5 its curvature is negative, so the equimolar mixture lowers G by splitting into two phases.

spec.aria: Plot of molar Gibbs energy of mixing against x₁ for A = 0, 1.5 and 2.5; the A = 2.5 curve rises in the middle, so a mixture near x₁ = 0.5 lowers its energy by splitting into two phases.

examples.question: At 300 K and 1 bar, the molar Gibbs energy of mixing of a binary liquid is g^M/RT = x₁ ln x₁ + x₂ ln x₂ + A x₁x₂ with A = 2.5. Test the equimolar mixture (x₁ = 0.5) for stability.
steps: First derivative: ln(x₁/x₂) + A(1 − 2x₁) = ln(1) + 2.5(1 − 1) = 0. The point is stationary.
The value is negative, so G curves downward at x₁ = 0.5. A small split into two compositions lowers G; the mixture is unstable.
examples.answer: The equimolar mixture is unstable because d²(g^M/RT)/dx₁² = −1.0 < 0; it splits, and g^M/RT at x₁ = 0.5 is −0.0681.
examples.check:
import math
A = 2.5
x = 0.5
x2 = 1 - x
d2 = 1/x + 1/x2 - 2*A
gmix = x*math.log(x) + x2*math.log(x2) + A*x*x2
print(round(d2, 4))
print(round(gmix, 4))

traps: Equating partial pressures p_i instead of fugacities f_i. At high pressure the fugacity coefficient φ_i changes the answer: f_i = φ_i y_i P in a gas.
Calling a mixture stable because the first derivative of G is zero. A stationary point can be a maximum or a saddle; the second derivative must be positive.
Confusing fugacity f_i (Pa) with fugacity coefficient φ_i (dimensionless). They differ by pressure and composition.
Calling the spinodal the phase boundary. The actual coexisting compositions come from the binodal, the common tangent where μ_i is equal in both phases.
Using a pure-component standard state when the problem needs a Henry standard state for a dilute solute; the activity definition and the numerical fugacity change.

quiz.q: State the three equilibrium equalities for phases α and β.
quiz.a: Thermal: T^α = T^β. Mechanical: P^α = P^β. Chemical: μ_i^α = μ_i^β, equivalently f_i^α = f_i^β, for every component i.

quiz.q: Why is fugacity used instead of chemical potential in phase-equilibrium calculations?
quiz.a: Chemical potential contains an arbitrary reference value. Fugacity is defined through μ_i = μ_i° + RT ln(f_i/f_i°). For the same component the reference cancels, so equality of μ becomes equality of f. Fugacity also has pressure units and connects directly to measurable P, x and y.

quiz.q: For a binary mixture, g^M/RT = x₁ ln x₁ + x₂ ln x₂ + A x₁x₂ with A = 1.5. Compute the second derivative at x₁ = 0.5 and classify the mixture.
quiz.a: x₂ = 0.5. d²(g^M/RT)/dx₁² = 1/x₁ + 1/x₂ − 2A = 2 + 2 − 3 = 1.0. The value is positive, so the equimolar mixture is locally stable.

quiz.q: At A = 2.5 and x₁ = 0.5 the first derivative is zero but the mixture is unstable. Explain what the second derivative shows.
quiz.a: The first derivative being zero only makes x₁ = 0.5 stationary. The second derivative is −1.0, so G curves downward there. Any small composition change lowers G, and the system lowers G further by splitting into two phases whose compositions lie on the common tangent.

quiz.q: Define spinodal and binodal in a binary mixture.
quiz.a: The spinodal is the locus where (∂²G/∂x₁²)_{T,P} = 0. The binodal gives the compositions of two coexisting phases, found from the common tangent or equal chemical potentials.

quiz.q: Why can a curved interface have P^α ≠ P^β while a flat interface cannot?
quiz.a: Surface tension at a curved interface supports a pressure jump, often written ΔP = 2γ/r for a spherical droplet, with γ in N/m and r in m. For a flat interface r → ∞, so the pressure jump goes to zero and P^α = P^β.

quiz.q: A binary mixture has (∂²G/∂x₁²)_{T,P} = +2.0 kJ/mol at a stationary composition. Is it stable? What if the value is −2.0 kJ/mol?
quiz.a: Positive curvature means a local minimum of G, so the mixture is locally stable. Negative curvature means a maximum or saddle in the composition direction, so it is unstable and tends to split. The units are kJ/mol because G is per mole and x₁ is dimensionless.

quiz.q: A student finds μ_i^α = μ_i^β for every component but T^α ≠ T^β. Is the system at phase equilibrium?
quiz.a: No. Phase equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical equality together. If temperatures differ, heat can flow and G can fall; the chemical equality alone does not make the whole system equilibrium.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same curvature test predicts spinodal decomposition in polymer blends, metal alloys and pharmaceutical amorphous solid dispersions. In enhanced oil recovery, phase-stability calculations decide whether injected CO₂ forms one phase or splits into oil-rich and water-rich phases. Process simulators solve the fugacity equalities together with the stability test before they report a bubble point or a tie line. Search next for 'spinodal decomposition', 'tangent plane distance stability test', and 'phase stability in CO₂ capture solvents'.
